title: I Took the Anodizing-Tank Booking to the Tech Who Palmed My Racks

parts.text: I stepped into tank B at 11:03 a.m. and tech Wren was already using my numbered racks. The board said: FIFTY MINUTES. RACKS STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty-one, finishing lead, holding a clipboard that listed our dye. Wren shrugged. "Techs keep the tank." I photographed the board, the booking, and her parts on my racks. Then I asked for the tank booking. At 11:11 the ano desk pinged why Wren's parts sat on our racks. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The ano desk can see Wren's parts in tank B during our dye.

social.video_title: She palmed my numbered anodizing racks — Part 1/2
social.description: Anodizing tank, a tech on my racks, a fifty-minute clock she posted. I logged the parts. Would you have asked for the tank booking?

parts.text: Wren called it color tests until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the tank still. The racks went back to my numbered bar. Wren ran a slot of their own and told the next tech atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: TECHS DO NOT KEEP THE TANK. I keep our dye on a labeled card. Wren brown-bags her parts. The tank finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Techs do not keep the tank — Part 2/2
social.description: Tank booking, numbered racks, and a second line on the board. Were color tests ever our dye?
